back: Officially authorizes the project and gives the project manager authority to allocate resources, typically through a charter.
Issued by the initiator or sponsor; formally authorizes the project and the project manager's use of resources.

front: When to assign the project manager
back: As early as possible, ideally while the charter is developed, and always before planning begins.
An economic feasibility study that justifies the project; used throughout the life cycle and after completion.
How and when benefits will be delivered, and how they will be measured; target benefits (e.g. NPV).
All assumptions and constraints throughout the project; high-level ones start in the business case and charter.
Light; answers why, who will be engaged, what, where, when, how, and who the customer is.
Contracts set the agreement between organizations; charters are used inside each one.
Sustainability KPIs can go into the charter, business case, scope statement and contracts, then be monitored.
At the start, as part of the project management plan: metrics for scope, schedule, budget and quality.
Integrates and aligns all plan components into one project management plan; done once or at intervals.

front: First job of Integrate and Align
back: Establish the tailoring, the development approach and the life cycle; they guide planning in every domain.
How the project will be executed, monitored and controlled, and closed. The basis for all decisions; a living document.
Change, communications, financial, procurement, quality, requirements, resource, risk, schedule, scope, sourcing, engagement plans; iteration, release, test plans.
Approved scope statement, WBS and WBS dictionary; changed only through formal change control.
Approved schedule model with baseline start and finish dates; changed only through change control.
Approved time-phased budget including contingency reserves, excluding management reserves.
Establishes the change control board (steering committee), its authority, and how change control works.
Enough to move forward appropriately, not more detailed than necessary.
Identifies the type, quantity and characteristics of resources needed; anticipates shortages or surpluses.
How the estimate was derived: assumptions, constraints, detail, range (e.g. ±10%), confidence level, risks.
Verify alignment of all plans and baselines (dependencies, gaps) and that the business value still holds.
Leads and performs the planned work and implements approved changes: corrective, preventive, defect repair.
Data: raw observations (story points done, actual dates). Information: data compared with the plan.
Change it when that enhances value; changes to baselines always go through formal change control.
